name: Kasimir 'Casey' Dudek
languages: Polish (his first language, which he dreams in)
Croatian (well enough for the Strawberry Hill taverns)
equipment: Leather jacket, black, with a torn pocket he has sewn up himself, badly
Brass knuckles, in the right-hand pocket, which he says are for show
.45 automatic (Colt M1911, war surplus, bought from a man at the Burnham for $12), 7 rounds loaded, in his belt at the back
Hand wraps and a gym bag
A clipping from 1929: KID CASIMIR STOPS ST. JOE HEAVY IN SIXTH, and on the other side, KID CASIMIR LOSES DECISION TO BOWDEN
A good suit, a size too small in the shoulders, for funerals and court
Pack of cigarettes and a cigarette case with a dent in it
A rosary from his mother that he does not use and will not throw away
A key to room 41 at the Burnham Hotel, Fifth Street, which he has not been back to since Sunday
Fifty dollars in an envelope from Harvey Gleason, for 'finding a book', counted into the wallet
features: Two Languages (New Arrival origin: Polish and English fluently, Croatian well; people assume he understands less than he does, so advantage on Perception and Insight to follow a conversation in a language the speakers think he doesn't know; in any Polish or Croatian community he can find a meal, a bed and a rumour without a check)

Hard Knocks (Heavy: unarmed strikes deal 1d6 + STR; once per turn, +1d4 bludgeoning with an unarmed strike or a bludgeoning melee weapon; a creature he drops with one is knocked out unless he chooses otherwise; he can deliver knockout blows with fists)
Thick Skull (Heavy: advantage on CON saves against knockout blows and being stunned; once per long rest, drop to 1 hit point instead of 0)

The Look (Heavy, 2nd level: as an action, a creature within 30 ft that can see him makes a WIS save, DC 13, or is frightened of him until the end of his next turn; outside combat, a failed save means it answers one question truthfully or does one reasonable thing he says)
Style: Bruiser (Heavy, 3rd level: his unarmed strikes deal 1d8 instead, and when he takes the Attack action he can make one unarmed strike or grapple as a bonus action)

Fight Crowd (Prizefighter background: managers, trainers, promoters and gamblers know him; he can get a seat at any fight in town and name the bookmaker who takes the big bets. He fought on the same cards as Lucky Bowden in 1929, and lost to him on points)

personality.traits: I say very little and I watch hands. I fold my arms when I am thinking, which people take for a threat, which is useful. I go to Mass at Christmas and Easter and feel bad about the other fifty weeks.
personality.ideals: A man keeps his word, even when he gave it to the wrong people. Especially then, maybe. I am trying to work out whether that's true.
personality.bonds: My mother in Strawberry Hill, who thinks I work at the packing house. And my kid brother Stash, who is sixteen and wants to be just like me, God help him.
personality.flaws: I have voted eleven times in one day for two dollars a time, and in the spring of '34 I stood outside a polling place on Twelfth Street while men I came with beat a man to death for asking our names. I did not hit him. I did not stop it. I took my two dollars. I am still taking Gleason's money.

appearance: A big, heavy-shouldered white man of thirty-four with a flattened nose, a scar through his left eyebrow, cauliflowered ears, very pale blue eyes and fair hair cut short. He moves lightly for his size, like the fighter he was. Black leather jacket, flat cap, hands in his pockets.
backstory: Kasimir Dudek was born in a village outside Kraków in 1902 and came to Kansas City, Kansas, at eleven with his mother to join a father who had found work at the packing houses and died of influenza a year later. He grew up on Strawberry Hill above the rail yards, among Croatian and Polish families, left school at thirteen for the packing-house floor, and boxed as Kid Casimir from 1922 to 1931, a heavyweight with a good chin and a slow left, ninety fights, sixty wins. Black and white fighters were on the same cards in Kansas City and not in the same dressing rooms, and in 1929 he lost a ten-round decision at the Convention Hall to a young Black heavyweight named Lucky Bowden who later became a drummer, and they shook hands in the ring, and he has never forgotten it. When the fights ended so did the money, and since 1932 he has lived at the Burnham Hotel and done jobs for Harvey Gleason: collecting, standing in doorways, and every election, voting. On Sunday afternoon Gleason gave him fifty dollars to find 'a black book a colored piano player took off a gentleman'. He took the money. On Monday he found out which piano player, and whose band he played in, and he has been walking up and down Eighteenth Street ever since trying to decide what kind of man he is.
